newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ June qtr inflation risk on downside- economists.
newsitem.headline: NZ June qtr inflation risk on downside- economists.

text.p: The risks for next week's New Zealand inflation data lie firmly on the downside, opening up the prospect of a further market-led easing in monetary conditions, economists said on Wednesday.

June quarter Consumers Price Index data is due on Tuesday at 2245 GMT. The central bank has forecast quarterly core inflation of 0.3 percent, compared with an actual 0.22 percent in the March quarter. Latest Reserve Bank (RBNZ) forecasts predict underlying inflation will slip down to one percent in the March 1998 year, from 1.97 percent in the March 1997 year.
The RBNZ is mandated to keep core inflation within a zero to three percent target band.

Economists, who broadly agree with the Reserve Bank's June quarter forecast, said that although financial markets were rapped across the knuckles by the central bank last week for easing conditions too far, the easing bias was alive and well.
Even a quarterly inflation out-turn right on expectations of 0.3 percent would prompt markets to try their luck once more, they said.
Conditions are currently 57 basis points easier than the RBNZ's desired levels, but the bank has said it would tolerate a deviation of 50 points either side of its assumptions.
UBS Australia chief economist Stephen Roberts said sooner or later the RBNZ would have to bow to the inevitable and officially ease conditions further.

"I see them wanting to ease monetary conditions a lot over the course of the next six months or so. That's simply because the forecasting risk is on the side of lower growth and lower inflation," he said.
However, Roberts said the low inflation performance had come at the expense of growth, leaving the RBNZ open to the accusation of over-kill.
"There's a real risk that economic growth in New Zealand continues to travel around the low ranges of one point something over the next six to 12 months," he said.
"And that will be not only below the Reserve Bank's forecasts, but Treasury's forecasts as well."
Like the RBNZ, Treasury forecasts core inflation of one percent in the March 1998 year.
National Bank of New Zealand economist Kevin Smit said inflationary pressures were often overestimated during periods of slow economic activity such as the country was experiencing.
It was possible the RBNZ was slightly too aggressive in targeting one percent annual inflation in March 1998.
"There is some risk that you could come in a bit lower than that, and of course you don't have to come in much lower and you're right at the bottom end of the (target) band," Smit said.
"Even with this (June quarter) number...you'd have to say that with the economy slowing down as it has over the first half of this year, the risks are probably more on the downside."

Smit said that combined with sharply weaker-than-expected GDP data late in June, a surprisingly soft inflation out-turn might give the RBNZ grounds for revisiting whether its assumed monetary conditions were appropriate.
Much would depend on the size of the undershoot, he said.
